license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026–27 rates and include the mandatory $4 Habitat Management and Access Validation on top of the $35 resident and $90 non-resident annual licence. A further $10 Habitat Stamp is required to fish Forest Service or BLM land. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Tennessee
answer: Tennessee fly fishing is tailwater fishing below TVA dams plus native brook trout in the Smokies, with brown and rainbow trout as the mainstays. The South Holston, Watauga, Clinch and Caney Fork are the headline rivers. A licence is required from age 16, trout needs a supplemental licence, and the dam release schedule decides your day.
summary: The South Holston's sulphur hatch, which runs most of the year, plus Smokies brook trout. Check the TVA generation schedule before you drive.
whatMakesItDifferent: Tennessee's trout fishing was built by the Tennessee Valley Authority, and one piece of engineering explains the best of it. The South Holston has a labyrinth weir below the main dam, built to put oxygen back into water drawn from the bottom of the reservoir, and the oxygenated, cold, stable river below it produces a sulphur hatch that runs for most of the year rather than for three weeks in June. Anglers come from several states away to fish a mayfly hatch in February. The flip side is that every one of these rivers is operated for power generation: the water can rise several feet inside an hour, and wading becomes floating. Above the tailwaters sit the streams of the Great Smoky Mountains, which are the opposite in every respect — small, free-flowing, and holding the southernmost native brook trout in the country.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and self-sustaining in the South Holston and the Watauga.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Wild in the tailwaters and the Smokies, and stocked almost everywhere else.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native Southern Appalachian strain, in the highest and coldest Smokies streams.

species.name: Smallmouth bass
species.note: The warmer middle Tennessee rivers, and very good in their own right.

waters.name: South Holston River
waters.note: The sulphur hatch that made the state's reputation, and a slot limit protecting its wild browns.

waters.name: Watauga River
waters.note: The South Holston's neighbour. Bigger water, strong caddis, and fewer anglers.

waters.name: Clinch River
waters.note: Below Norris Dam. Famous for large browns and for the care its sulphurs demand.

waters.name: Caney Fork River
waters.note: Below Center Hill, within reach of Nashville. Generation-dependent and worth planning around.

waters.name: Hiwassee River
waters.note: Cherokee National Forest. Pocket water, wadeable at low flow, and genuinely scenic.

waters.name: Great Smoky Mountains streams
waters.note: Little River, Abrams Creek and the high brook trout water. A TN or NC licence is valid.

seasons.what: Sulphurs on the South Holston even in the cold, with midges and blue-wing olives alongside.
Quill Gordons and March browns in the Smokies, caddis on the tailwaters. The best weeks for both.
Heavy afternoon generation for power demand. Fish early, fish high in the mountains, or fish from a boat.
Flows settle, terrestrials come into their own, and the Smokies are at their best.
Brown trout spawn in the tailwaters. Stay off the gravel and watch for seasonal restrictions.

regulations: A licence is required from age 16, and a supplemental trout licence is required on top of it. Tennessee does not sell a resident fishing-only annual licence: a resident who wants to fish for trout buys the combination hunt and fish licence plus the trout supplemental.
The non-resident annual licence comes in two forms — with trout and without — and the trout version costs twice as much.
TVA sets the generation schedule, not the wildlife agency. Check releases before you travel and again before you wade.
The South Holston and other tailwaters carry slot limits and tackle restrictions protecting wild brown trout.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park has its own rules. A Tennessee or North Carolina licence is valid inside it.

license.priceNote: The resident total is the $33 combination hunt and fish annual licence plus the $21 annual trout supplemental — there is no resident fishing-only annual licence. The non-resident figure is the $98 annual all-species licence, which includes trout; a non-resident licence without trout is $49. Processing fees are extra. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Vermont
answer: Vermont fly fishing is small-river and mountain-stream fishing, with wild brown trout, native brook trout, rainbows and landlocked Atlantic salmon. The Battenkill, the White River and the Winooski are the headline waters. A licence is required from age 15, and the trout season on most streams runs from April into late October.
summary: The Battenkill, which humbles people, and Green Mountain brook trout streams. Manchester is where American fly fishing became a business.
whatMakesItDifferent: Manchester, Vermont is the commercial birthplace of American fly fishing. Orvis was founded there in 1856 and is still there, the American Museum of Fly Fishing is a few minutes away, and the Battenkill runs between them. That river is the most quietly difficult trout stream in the Northeast: cold, clear, low in nutrients, and holding wild brown trout in modest numbers that have seen a great many flies. Nobody fishes the Battenkill for numbers. What Vermont gives you instead, once you leave the valley, is an enormous amount of small wild water — hundreds of miles of Green Mountain brook trout streams that no guide books and almost nobody fishes, reached by pulling off a dirt road and walking upstream. The state is small enough that both are a morning's drive apart.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native, and the default fish in the mountain streams. Small, bright and abundant.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild in the Battenkill and the larger valley rivers, and not easily fooled.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: The White River and the Winooski hold wild, strong, lake-run fish in spring.

species.name: Landlocked Atlantic salmon
species.note: Lake Champlain and Lake Memphremagog tributaries, running in spring and autumn.

waters.name: Battenkill River
waters.note: Famously hard. Wild browns, gin-clear water and a long history of humility.

waters.name: White River
waters.note: A long free-flowing river with wild rainbows and a run of lake fish in spring.

waters.name: Winooski River
waters.note: Lake Champlain tributary. Steelhead and landlocked salmon below the falls.

waters.name: Lamoille River
waters.note: Mixed browns and rainbows, good hatches, and easier than the Battenkill.

waters.name: Otter Creek
waters.note: Slower, warmer water holding big browns and, lower down, pike.

waters.name: Clyde River
waters.note: Northeast Kingdom. Landlocked salmon running out of Memphremagog in autumn.

seasons.what: The general trout season opens on the second Saturday. High cold water, and nymphs more than dries.
Hendricksons, then caddis. The rivers drop and the dry-fly fishing starts in earnest.
The best month. Sulphurs, March browns and evening caddis on every river in the state.
Low water. Fish the mountain brook trout streams and the terrestrials, and go early.
Landlocked salmon running, brown trout colouring up, and the season closing at the end of October on most streams.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 15.
Most trout streams run a season from the second Saturday in April to the end of October. A number of waters are open year-round, and some are catch and release outside the season.
Vermont has designated trout management areas with their own tackle and harvest rules — check the stretch before you fish it.
Landlocked salmon and lake trout carry their own seasons and limits on the Champlain and Memphremagog tributaries.

license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026 rates for an annual fishing licence, and match the fee schedule set in Vermont statute. There is no separate trout stamp. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Maine
answer: Maine fly fishing is remote pond and river fishing for native brook trout and landlocked Atlantic salmon, with some wild browns and rainbows in the south. The Rapid River, Grand Lake Stream, the Kennebec and the Moosehead ponds are the headline waters. A licence is required from age 16, and the season turns on ice-out rather than on a calendar.
summary: Nearly all of America's remaining wild brook trout ponds are in Maine. Landlocked salmon on streamers at ice-out, and water you reach by canoe.
whatMakesItDifferent: Maine holds something no other state does. The great majority of the United States' remaining wild, self-sustaining brook trout *ponds* are inside its borders — hundreds of small cold waters in the north and west that have never been stocked and never needed to be, holding native brook trout in the landscape they evolved in. Reaching them means a logging road, a canoe on the roof and no mobile signal, which is exactly why they still exist. The state's other tradition is the streamer. Landlocked Atlantic salmon chase smelt into the rivers as soon as the ice goes out in May, and the Maine streamer patterns tied to imitate those smelt — long, slim, feather-winged — are an American fly-tying school in their own right. Both of these are calendar-proof: here you plan a trip around ice-out, not around a date.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native and wild, in rivers and in hundreds of unstocked ponds. The reason to come.

species.name: Landlocked Atlantic salmon
species.note: Chasing smelt at ice-out, and jumping more than a trout has any right to.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Southern and central rivers, and some of the larger lakes.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Less widespread, chiefly in the south.

species.name: Lake trout
species.note: Called togue here. Deep lakes, and reachable on a fly at ice-out.

waters.name: Rapid River
waters.note: Between Richardson and Umbagog. Big wild brook trout and heavy, hard wading.

waters.name: Grand Lake Stream
waters.note: Three miles of landlocked salmon water, and the birthplace of the Grand Laker canoe.

waters.name: Kennebec — East Outlet
waters.note: Below Moosehead Lake. Salmon and brook trout in powerful water.

waters.name: Roach River
waters.note: Fly fishing only, with salmon and brook trout running out of Moosehead in autumn.

waters.name: West Branch Penobscot
waters.note: Below Ripogenus. Famous salmon water and genuinely remote.

waters.name: The remote ponds
waters.note: Hundreds of unstocked brook trout waters in the north and west, reached by road and canoe.

seasons.what: Ice-out. Streamers for landlocked salmon chasing smelt — the most Maine fishing there is.
The best weeks. Hatches on the ponds, brook trout rising, and the blackflies at their worst.
Warm water pushes fish deep. Head north, fish the spring holes, and fish early and late.
Salmon and brook trout run up the rivers to spawn. Cold mornings and the best river fishing of the year.
Most waters close at the end of September, with extended catch-and-release water into October and ice fishing after that.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 16.
Many waters are designated fly fishing only or artificial lures only, and those designations are listed water by water in the law book rather than applied statewide.
Using live fish as bait is prohibited on a long list of waters, to protect native brook trout from introduced species. The prohibition is taken seriously.
General open-water season on most waters runs from 1 April to 30 September, with extended catch-and-release seasons on some rivers into October.
The rules are set per water with codes in the law book. Look up the pond or stream before you drive to it.

license.agency: Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife
license.priceNote: Figures are the 2026 rates for a season fishing licence, ages 16 and over, and exclude the agent fee. They match the fee schedule set in Maine statute. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Virginia
answer: Virginia fly fishing is native brook trout fishing in mountain headwaters, with limestone spring creeks in the Valley and tailwaters below the big dams. Shenandoah National Park, Mossy Creek and the Jackson River are the headline waters. A licence is required from age 16, and a separate trout licence is needed only on designated stocked waters.
summary: Native brook trout in Shenandoah National Park, a limestone spring creek at Mossy Creek, and tailwater browns on the Jackson and the Smith.
whatMakesItDifferent: Shenandoah National Park has around seventy wild brook trout streams inside it, and they are the point of fishing in Virginia. They are small — a rod length across in places — steep, overhung with rhododendron, and they hold native Southern Appalachian brook trout that have never been stocked over. Fishing them is short casts, a lot of climbing and a lot of looking at where not to put your feet, and the fish rarely reach ten inches. Nobody who does it regularly cares. The useful thing to understand about Virginia is that its licensing follows this split exactly: the separate trout licence is required only on designated *stocked* trout waters. The wild brook trout streams in the park and the national forests need the ordinary freshwater licence and nothing more, which makes the best fishing in the state also the cheapest.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native Southern Appalachian strain, wild in the mountain headwaters. Rarely large, and worth the walk.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The Jackson and Smith tailwaters, and Mossy Creek, where they get genuinely big.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Wild in some mountain streams and stocked through much of the rest.

species.name: Smallmouth bass
species.note: The James, the New and the Shenandoah. Excellent, and the right answer in July.

waters.name: Shenandoah National Park streams
waters.note: The Rapidan, Hughes River and Jeremys Run among about seventy. Native brook trout, single hook, mostly catch and release.

waters.name: Mossy Creek
waters.note: A limestone spring creek in the Valley. Large browns, no cover for the angler, and a long leader.

waters.name: Jackson River
waters.note: Tailwater below Gathright Dam. Cold all summer, with wild browns and a contested access history.

waters.name: Smith River
waters.note: Below Philpott Dam. A long cold tailwater holding wild brown trout.

waters.name: Rapidan River
waters.note: Herbert Hoover built his summer camp on it for the fishing. Still native brook trout water.

waters.name: James River
waters.note: Not trout, but the best smallmouth river in the state and a proper summer alternative.

seasons.what: Stocked water is being stocked, and the tailwaters fish. Cold, quiet and uncrowded.
The mountain streams wake up. Quill Gordons, blue quills and the first good brook trout fishing.
The best weeks. Caddis, sulphurs and March browns, and Mossy Creek before the weed takes over.
Hot and low. Fish terrestrials high in the mountains early, or switch to smallmouth on the James.
Cooling water, terrestrials holding on, autumn stocking from October, and brook trout in spawning colour.

regulations: A freshwater fishing licence is required from age 16.

A separate trout licence is required in addition on designated stocked trout waters. It is not required to fish wild, unstocked trout water — which includes most of the national park and national forest brook trout streams.
Shenandoah National Park requires a Virginia licence, and its own rules sit on top: artificial lures with a single hook, and catch and release on most streams.
Some fee fishing areas need a separate daily permit on top of the licence.
Special regulation waters — Mossy Creek among them — carry their own tackle and harvest rules and sometimes require landowner permission. Check before you go.

license.priceNote: Figures are the current published rates for a one-year freshwater licence plus the trout licence — $28 and $28 for residents, $72 and $48 for non-residents. The trout licence is only needed on designated stocked trout waters, so an angler fishing wild brook trout streams pays the freshwater figure alone. Issuance fees are included. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Alaska
answer: Alaska fly fishing is trout fishing driven by salmon, with enormous wild rainbow trout, Dolly Varden, Arctic grayling and five species of Pacific salmon. Bristol Bay, the Kenai and the Naknek are the headline waters. A licence is required from 18 for residents and 16 for visitors, and the season runs from June into October.
summary: Rainbow trout that follow spawning salmon and feed on their eggs. Bristol Bay in September is the biggest trout fishing in North America.
whatMakesItDifferent: Everywhere else, a trout river feeds its trout. In Alaska the ocean does it. Millions of salmon return to spawn each summer, and the rainbow trout, char and grayling organise their entire year around that arrival — holding behind spawning sockeye, eating loose eggs through the autumn, then eating the flesh of dead fish after the run collapses. It is why a Bristol Bay rainbow can reach thirty inches in a river that freezes for half the year, and why the biggest trout of the season come in September, behind the salmon, rather than in the warm months. It also sets what the fishing looks like: egg patterns and flesh flies more than mayflies, heavy tippet, and in many places a float plane because there is no road. Plan around the run, not around the weather, and treat bears as a certainty rather than a risk.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: The Bristol Bay fish are the largest wild rainbows in the world, and mostly catch and release.

species.name: Dolly Varden
species.note: Native char, abundant and often overlooked. They follow the salmon as closely as the rainbows do.

species.name: Arctic grayling
species.note: Widespread in the clear interior streams. Willing, beautiful, and happy to take a dry fly.

species.name: Sockeye salmon
species.note: The run that feeds everything else. Peak in June and July.

species.name: King salmon
species.note: The largest Pacific salmon, and the one that needs its own stamp.

species.name: Silver salmon
species.note: August into October, and the most willing of the salmon to chase a fly.

waters.name: Naknek River
waters.note: Bristol Bay. Very large rainbows, and heavy water that fishes best from a boat.

waters.name: Kvichak River
waters.note: Drains Lake Iliamna. The classic big-rainbow river, fished behind the sockeye.

waters.name: Alagnak River
waters.note: A wild and scenic river with braided water and every species in it.

waters.name: Kenai River
waters.note: Road accessible from Anchorage, which is rare here. Big rainbows and a lot of company.

waters.name: Brooks River
waters.note: Katmai National Park. Famous fishing and famous bears, in the same hundred yards.

waters.name: Talachulitna River
waters.note: A fly-out river north of Anchorage, with rainbows, grayling and silvers.

seasons.what: The season opens. Rainbows recovering after spawning, grayling rising, and the first sockeye arriving.
Peak sockeye. Mouse patterns and leeches for rainbows before the eggs start coming.
Eggs everywhere, and silver salmon arriving. Fishing gets easier and busier.
The best weeks of the year. Big rainbows feeding hard on eggs and flesh, and the crowds thinning.
Freeze-up. Most lodges close by early October and the rivers are ice until late spring.

regulations: Residents need a licence from age 18; non-residents from age 16.
A king salmon stamp is required to fish for king salmon, including catch and release. It is not needed for trout, char or grayling.
Many of the best rainbow waters are catch and release with single barbless hooks, and some are fly fishing only. The rules are set river by river.
Emergency orders open and close fisheries in-season, sometimes within a day, in response to salmon escapement. Check before you fly.
Bears are not a hazard to plan around later. Fish with other people, carry deterrent, and give a fish you have hooked up if a bear wants it.

license.agency: Alaska Department of Fish and Game
license.priceNote: Figures are ADF&G's 2026 rates for an annual sport fishing licence. Non-residents can also buy 1, 3, 7 and 14-day licences for $15, $30, $45 and $75. A king salmon stamp is extra — $10 for residents, $100 for a non-resident annual — and is only needed to fish for kings. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Arizona
answer: Arizona fly fishing is a desert tailwater at Lees Ferry and native trout streams in the White Mountains, holding rainbow, brown and brook trout plus the native Apache and Gila trout. Lees Ferry, the Black River and Silver Creek are the headline waters. A licence is required from age 10, and Lees Ferry fishes all year.
summary: Lees Ferry — fifteen miles of cold clear tailwater in red rock desert — and the Apache trout, the first sport fish ever recovered off the endangered list.
whatMakesItDifferent: Arizona has the most improbable trout river in the country. Below Glen Canyon Dam the Colorado runs out at around forty-eight degrees, clear and cold, through red sandstone at the top of the Grand Canyon, and the fifteen miles down to Lees Ferry hold a dense population of rainbow trout in a landscape with saguaro an hour away. Most of it is fished by running a boat upstream from the ferry and wading the gravel bars, because there is no road along the bank. The state's other distinction is quieter and more important. The Apache trout, Arizona's state fish, was listed as endangered in 1967, and in September 2024 it became the first sport fish and the first trout in the United States ever removed from the endangered species list because it had recovered. You can fish for it, in the White Mountain streams it came from.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Lees Ferry holds them in numbers, and the high country is stocked with them.

species.name: Apache trout
species.note: The state fish, native to the White Mountains. Delisted in 2024 after fifty years of recovery work.

species.name: Gila trout
species.note: Native to a handful of southeastern streams, and fishable only where it is specifically allowed.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The Black River and some of the larger high-country streams.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Small, cold White Mountain creeks and lakes.

waters.name: Lees Ferry
waters.note: Fifteen miles of Colorado River tailwater below Glen Canyon Dam. Boat up, wade the bars, fish all year.

waters.name: Black River
waters.note: White Mountains. Wild browns and Apache trout in genuinely remote canyon water.

waters.name: Silver Creek
waters.note: A small spring-fed creek near Show Low, managed for Apache trout and fished hard in winter.

waters.name: West Fork Little Colorado
waters.note: Apache trout water on Mount Baldy, above 9,000 feet.

waters.name: Oak Creek
waters.note: Through Sedona. Scenic, accessible, busy, and better early in the day.

waters.name: Big Lake
waters.note: High-country stillwater at 9,000 feet. Cool all summer when the desert is unbearable.

seasons.what: Lees Ferry at its best — cold air, warm water, midges, and very few boats.
The high country is still under snow. Lees Ferry and the lower creeks carry the season.
Hot and dry. Fish Lees Ferry early, or get to 9,000 feet in the White Mountains.
Monsoon. Afternoon storms blow out the small streams in an hour, but they also cool everything down.
The best weeks in the high country before it closes in, and Lees Ferry settling into winter form.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 10 on any publicly accessible water in the state. A licence is valid one year from the date of purchase.
Lees Ferry has its own tackle and harvest rules, and the walk-in area at the ferry fishes differently from the water upstream.
Apache trout waters are managed under a cooperative plan between the state, the White Mountain Apache Tribe and federal agencies. Some are open, some are not.
Much of the best White Mountain water is on the Fort Apache Reservation, which issues its own permits. An Arizona licence does not cover it.
Rules are set water by water in the annual fishing regulations.

license.priceNote: Figures are the general fishing licence rates published in Arizona's own fishing regulations. The licence runs one year from the date you buy it rather than to a fixed date. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Missouri
answer: Missouri fly fishing is spring-fed trout park fishing and Ozark tailwater fishing, with rainbow and brown trout and a few streams of genuinely wild fish. The four trout parks, Lake Taneycomo and the Current River are the headline waters. A licence is required from age 16, trout need a permit or a daily tag, and the parks open on 1 March.
summary: Four spring-fed trout parks that open with a siren on 1 March, Lake Taneycomo below Table Rock, and wild McCloud-strain rainbows in Crane Creek.
whatMakesItDifferent: Missouri's trout fishing begins with a siren. Four state trout parks sit on enormous cold springs — Bennett Spring, Montauk, Roaring River and Maramec Spring — and at 6.30 on the morning of 1 March a whistle sounds and several thousand people start fishing at once. It is a genuine American tradition, closer to an opening-day football crowd than to a quiet morning on a creek, and the parks are stocked daily through the season for it. You buy a daily trout tag at the gate rather than an annual trout permit. Away from that noise the state hides something much rarer: Crane Creek, a small Ozark stream holding wild rainbow trout descended from the original McCloud River stock brought from California in the 1880s — a strain largely lost in its home water and still swimming here, in a creek you can step across.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Stocked heavily in the parks and the tailwaters; wild and McCloud-strain in a few Ozark creeks.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Lake Taneycomo and the North Fork of the White, where they reach serious size.

species.name: Smallmouth bass
species.note: The Ozark float streams, and the right answer from June to September.

waters.name: Bennett Spring State Park
waters.note: The busiest of the trout parks. Enormous spring flow, daily stocking, and a crowd on opening day.

waters.name: Montauk State Park
waters.note: The headwaters of the Current River. Park water above, wild-ish water below.

waters.name: Lake Taneycomo
waters.note: Cold water from the bottom of Table Rock. Not really a lake where it fishes — a big trout river.

waters.name: Current River
waters.note: Below Montauk. A clear Ozark river holding trout up top and smallmouth below.

waters.name: Crane Creek
waters.note: Wild rainbows descended from 1880s McCloud River stock. Tiny water, spooky fish, and no stocking.

waters.name: North Fork of the White River
waters.note: Wild rainbows and large browns in a classic Ozark spring-fed river.

seasons.what: Opening day in the trout parks. A siren, a crowd, and a tradition worth seeing once.
The parks in full swing, and the best wild-stream fishing of the year as the water warms.
Hot. Fish the springs and the tailwater early, or float an Ozark river for smallmouth instead.
Cooling water and the parks quieter. The last weeks of the regular park season run to 31 October.
Catch-and-release season in the parks, flies only, Friday to Monday. Taneycomo fishes all winter.

regulations: A fishing permit is required from age 16.
A trout permit is required to possess trout, except in the trout parks, where you buy a daily trout tag at the park instead.
A trout permit is required for the winter catch-and-release season in the parks, and year-round on Lake Taneycomo above the US 65 bridge.
The regular trout park season runs 1 March to 31 October. The winter catch-and-release season is flies only and runs on limited days.
Blue Ribbon, Red Ribbon and White Ribbon trout areas each carry their own tackle and harvest rules.

license.priceNote: The totals are the 2026 annual fishing permit plus the trout permit — $14 and $12 for residents, $57 and $24 for non-residents. Both rose for 2026, and the non-resident trout permit is new. In the trout parks you buy a daily trout tag instead of the trout permit. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Georgia
answer: Georgia fly fishing is north Georgia mountain stream fishing plus a cold tailwater running through metropolitan Atlanta, holding rainbow, brown and native brook trout. The Chattahoochee, the Toccoa and the Chattooga are the headline waters. A licence is required from age 16, and trout needs a separate trout licence.
summary: A genuine trout river inside Atlanta, delayed-harvest water that fishes all winter, and native brook trout in headwaters above 2,000 feet.
whatMakesItDifferent: Georgia has a wild brown trout fishery inside a city of six million people. Buford Dam releases water from the bottom of Lake Lanier at around fifty degrees, and the Chattahoochee stays cold all the way down through the northern suburbs and into Atlanta — you can fish a hatch within sight of an interstate, and in August, when the rest of the Southeast is too warm for trout, it is one of the few places still fishing. Upstream, the north Georgia mountains hold the other half of the state: hundreds of miles of small Blue Ridge streams, native brook trout in the coldest and highest of them, and a delayed-harvest programme that turns several ordinary rivers into excellent catch-and-release fly water from November into May. Georgia's trout season is effectively the opposite of most states': the good months are the cold ones.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild in the Chattahoochee tailwater and several mountain rivers, and large in the Soque.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Wild in much of the north Georgia water, stocked through the rest.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native Southern Appalachian strain, in small high headwater streams above about 2,000 feet.

species.name: Striped bass
species.note: In the lower Chattahoochee in summer — a different fish and a different rod, but they are there.

waters.name: Chattahoochee River
waters.note: Buford Dam down through Atlanta. A cold tailwater inside a metropolitan area, fishable all summer.

waters.name: Toccoa River tailwater
waters.note: Below Blue Ridge Dam. Wild browns, generation-dependent, and the best big-fish water in the state.

waters.name: Chattooga River
waters.note: Wild and Scenic, on the South Carolina line. Remote, rocky and worth the walk in.

waters.name: Soque River
waters.note: Almost entirely private and fished by the day. Large trout, and you pay for the privilege.

waters.name: Dukes Creek
waters.note: Smithgall Woods. Reservation only, catch and release, and quiet in a way few southern streams are.

waters.name: Noontootla Creek
waters.note: Blue Ridge wild trout water, artificial lures only, with a long-standing size limit.

seasons.what: Delayed-harvest water opens 1 November and fishes beautifully from the first week.
The Chattahoochee tailwater and the delayed-harvest rivers. Midges, small nymphs, almost nobody out.
The mountain streams come alive. Quill Gordons, Hendricksons and caddis, and the brookies waking up.
The last weeks of delayed harvest, which ends 14 May, and the best hatches of the year.
Too warm for most mountain streams by day. Fish the tailwaters, or go high and early.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 16, and a separate trout licence is required in addition to fish for trout.
Delayed-harvest water is artificial lures only and catch and release from 1 November to 14 May.
Some waters are artificial-lures-only or carry size limits year-round, and a few of the best are reservation-only.
The Chattooga is shared with South Carolina, and a licence from either state is valid on the main river — but not on its tributaries.
Rules are set stream by stream. Check the water before you fish it.

license.agency: Georgia Department of Natural Resources, Wildlife Resources Division
license.priceNote: The totals are the annual fishing licence plus the annual trout licence — $15 and $10 for residents, $50 and $25 for non-residents. The trout licence is required for any mountain trout fishing. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.

name: Minnesota
answer: Minnesota holds three separate trout fisheries: Driftless spring creeks in the southeast, Lake Superior tributaries on the North Shore, and wilderness brook trout lakes in the north. Brown, brook and rainbow trout and steelhead are the quarry. A licence and a trout stamp are required from age 16, and the southeast opens for catch and release on 1 January.
summary: Driftless spring creeks in the southeast, North Shore steelhead, and brook trout lakes you reach by canoe. Three fisheries in one state.
whatMakesItDifferent: Most states have one trout fishery. Minnesota has three, and they have almost nothing to do with each other. The southeast corner is Driftless country — the same unglaciated limestone geology as western Wisconsin, with hundreds of spring creeks holding wild brown trout, and a winter catch-and-release season that opens on 1 January while the rest of the state is frozen solid. Two hundred and fifty miles north, the streams of the Lake Superior shore drop off the Sawtooth Mountains in a series of waterfalls, and steelhead run up into them in spring as far as the first impassable falls. North of that again, the Arrowhead and the Boundary Waters hold brook trout in small, cold, stocked-once-and-left lakes that you reach by paddling and portaging. One licence covers all three, and no single trip could sensibly take in more than one.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: Wild and abundant in the southeast spring creeks, and the main quarry there.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Native. The coldest southeast headwaters and the wilderness lakes in the north.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Stocked in the southeast, and the resident form of the North Shore steelhead.

species.name: Steelhead
species.note: Lake Superior fish running the North Shore streams in spring.

species.name: Lake trout
species.note: Deep Boundary Waters lakes, reachable on a fly just after ice-out.

waters.name: Whitewater River
waters.note: The best-known southeast spring creek system, with state park and easement access.

waters.name: Root River
waters.note: A long southeast valley system with wild browns and good hatches.

waters.name: Hay Creek
waters.note: Near Red Wing. Small, close to the Twin Cities and fished accordingly.

waters.name: Knife River
waters.note: North Shore. Steelhead in spring, up to the falls and no further.

waters.name: Baptism River
waters.note: Drops off the Sawtooths into Superior. Steep, rocky steelhead water.

waters.name: Boundary Waters brook trout lakes
waters.note: Small stocked lakes reached by canoe and portage. Quiet in a way nowhere else is.

seasons.what: The southeast catch-and-release season. Midges on spring creeks that steam in the cold.
The harvest season opens in the southeast, and steelhead run the North Shore. The busiest weeks of the year.
Hatches in the southeast, ice-out fishing in the north, and the blackflies arriving with both.
Hopper season on the spring creeks. Low clear water, and fish the evenings.
Tricos and Baetis, then the season closing and the winter catch-and-release water taking over.

regulations: A fishing licence is required from age 16, and a trout and salmon stamp validation is required in addition for designated trout streams and lakes and for Lake Superior.
Annual licences run from 1 March to the end of February.
The southeast winter season is catch and release with artificial lures, opening 1 January ahead of the general harvest season in April.
North Shore steelhead are managed tightly, with wild fish released and rules differing between streams.
Boundary Waters trout lakes carry their own access rules and, in some cases, permit requirements for entry.

name: Nevada
answer: Nevada fly fishing is desert lake and Great Basin stream fishing, with Lahontan cutthroat, rainbow, brown and brook trout. Pyramid Lake, the Truckee and the East Walker are the headline waters. A state licence is required from age 12, but Pyramid Lake is tribal water and needs a permit from the Paiute Tribe instead.
summary: Pyramid Lake, where anglers fish from stepladders for the largest cutthroat trout on earth, and tailwater browns on the East Walker.
whatMakesItDifferent: Pyramid Lake is unlike any other trout fishery in the world. It is a desert terminal lake north of Reno, the remnant of an inland sea, and it holds Lahontan cutthroat trout that grow past twenty pounds — the largest cutthroat on earth. The strain fishing there now was thought extinct for decades until a relict population was found in a small creek on the Utah border and brought back. The fishing is strange to watch and stranger to do: anglers stand on aluminium stepladders in the shallows, several feet above the water, casting out over a drop-off they otherwise could not reach. And it is not state water. The lake lies entirely within the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation and is fished on a permit issued by the Tribe, bought from the Tribe, under the Tribe's rules — not Nevada's. Buy it from them and ask them what else you need.

species.name: Lahontan cutthroat
species.note: Native to the Great Basin, and at Pyramid Lake the largest cutthroat trout anywhere.

species.name: Brown trout
species.note: The East Walker and the Truckee, where they get large and sulky.

species.name: Rainbow trout
species.note: Widespread in the rivers and the stocked mountain lakes.

species.name: Brook trout
species.note: Small high streams in the Rubies and the Jarbidge country.

species.name: Bull trout
species.note: The Jarbidge River holds the southernmost population in the world. Protected — do not target them.

waters.name: Pyramid Lake
waters.note: Tribal water, tribal permit. Stepladders, shooting heads and the biggest cutthroat in the world.

waters.name: Truckee River
waters.note: Out of Tahoe and through Reno. Big browns, technical water, and more of it public than people expect.

waters.name: East Walker River
waters.note: Below Bridgeport Reservoir. A tailwater holding heavy browns, shared with California.

waters.name: Ruby Mountains lakes
waters.note: Alpine lakes above Lamoille Canyon, reached on foot. Brook and rainbow trout.

waters.name: Jarbidge River
waters.note: Remote northeastern canyon water, and the southernmost bull trout on earth.

waters.name: Angel Lake
waters.note: A high cirque lake near Wells. Easy to reach and cold in midsummer.

seasons.what: Pyramid Lake's season opens. Cold, windy, and the fish moving into the shallows.
The best weeks at Pyramid for a big fish. Dress for standing still in a desert winter.
Pyramid finishes at the end of June. Mountain streams start as the snow leaves.
High country and tailwaters only. The East Walker fishes on dam releases through the heat.
Cooling water, brown trout colouring up on the Truckee, and the alpine lakes at their best.

regulations: A Nevada fishing licence is required from age 12 for state waters.

Pyramid Lake lies entirely within the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation and is fished on a permit issued by the Tribe. Buy it from the Tribe, follow their rules and seasons, and ask them directly what else is required — do not assume a Nevada licence covers you there.
Pyramid Lake is artificial flies and lures with barbless hooks, and has its own season and slot limits set by the Tribe.
Bull trout in the Jarbidge drainage are protected and may not be targeted.
The East Walker is shared with California, and the state line matters. Check which licence you need for the stretch you are standing in.

license.priceNote: Figures are NDOW's published rates for an annual adult fishing licence. There is no separate trout stamp. Pyramid Lake is not covered by this licence at all — it is tribal water with its own permit. Prices change — check with the agency before you buy.
